messages.author: 08e48595b188026f
messages.subject: Testing inequality hypotheses
parts:
Hi everyone,

I am trying to test a hypotheses if b1 > b2 > b3. 

I know I could potentially use chi-square difference tests (although then I would be testing b1 != b2 != b3) or by defining new parameters (e.g., b1b2 := b1 - b2), but is there a way to test the inequality hypotheses in "one go"? Similar to chi-square difference test?

I checked the restriktor package, but (as much as I understand) it uses ML as the estimator and listwise deletion, whereas I'd like to use MLR and FIML.

Any help/leads very appreciated!

Best,
Jošt

messages.author: d275eff513efeea3
messages.subject: Re: Testing inequality hypotheses
parts:
Hi Jošt,

This example demonstrates how to specify a model in lavaan and then apply restriktor to evaluate ordered hypotheses about the parameters using model selection:

Best,
Leonard

library(restriktor)

# lavaan syntax
model.lav <- "y1 ~ 1 + a*x1 + b*x2 + c*x3"
fit.lav <- sem(model.lav, data = PoliticalDemocracy)

# restriktor syntax
fit.restr <- goric(fit.lav, hypotheses = list(h1 = 'a > b > c'), comparison = "complement")
fit.restr

Dear Leonard,

Thank you for this example. I see this is the same/very similar as in the gorica package, and can probably help me in my analysis.

Just so I understand correctly: For lavaan objects, inequality hypotheses can be tested only with the goric function?
I saw in the documentation that one needs to use the restrictor and then iht functions to test the informative hypotheses. What got me confused is that for the restriktor function, it says that only lm, rlm and glm models are possible, and that the iht function requires a restriktor object as input (e.g., https://restriktor.org/tutorial/contest.html). However, in the documentation for iht function, there is mention of using lavaan objects and even such an example. I am now unsure if I can use iht with lavaan objects or not ... 

On a side note, what is the difference between goric and iht? If I understand correctly, goric evaluates and compares fit of different models, while iht provides actual statistical testing. Pointing me to an informative paper would be great (or, I can look for it myself once I find some time). Thanks, and sorry, I'm new to this! :)

Note though that my hypotheses are more in terms of a1 > a2 > a3 and b1 > b2 > b3 where
model = '
y1 ~ 1 + a1*x1 + b1*x2
y2 ~ 1 + a2*x1 + b2*x2
y3 ~ 1 + a3*x1 + b3*x2
'

Best,
Jošt

messages.author: d275eff513efeea3
messages.subject: Re: Testing inequality hypotheses
parts:
You can apply the iht() function to evaluate the order restricted hypothesis using hypothesis testing. 
It calls the bootstrapD() function designed for lavaan objects. This results in two hypothesis tests, often referred to as Type A and Type B, as detailed in 10.3389/fpsyg.2014.01565. However, it does not directly answer whether the order-restricted hypothesis holds in the population.
Moreover, the iht method is really slow for lavaan objects because it needs a double bootstrap procedure. You can speed things up using the parallel option, but 
still don't be afraid to go on a short holiday. 

h1 <- 'a1 > a2 > a3; b1 > b2 > b3'

model <- '

y1 ~ 1 + a1*x1 + b1*x2
  y2 ~ 1 + a2*x1 + b2*x2
  y3 ~ 1 + a3*x1 + b3*x2
'

iht(model = model, data = PoliticalDemocracy, constraints = h1,
    R = 1000, double.bootstrap = "no", parallel = "snow", ncpus = 8)

The advantage of the goric(a) is that you can directly evaluate your order-restricted hypothesis against its complement (i.e., not h1).

fit.lav <- sem(model, data = PoliticalDemocracy)
goric(fit.lav, hypotheses = list(h1 = h1), comparison = "complement")

From the results you can conclude that hypothesis h1 is 'some value' more supported than its complement.
See the Vignette in restriktor for "Guidelines interpretation GORIC(A) output" or feel free to contact me.

Leonard

Leonard,

Thank you for the clarifications and examples. Super helpful! I decided to first do a chi-square difference test to provide a statistical test of (non)equality of parameters, and then run the goric procedure to assess if the ordered hypotheses are better supported than the unconstrained ones.

Given the bootstrap and the associated computational demands, the iht method is not applicable for me since my model requires about 5 mins to be estimated as is (complex model with N > 1500 using FIML).

Thanks again and all the best!
Jošt
